claim: NY state real estate transfer tax: $2 for each $500 or fractional part of consideration on each conveyance of real property when consideration exceeds $500 (i.e., $2 per $500 = 0.4%). For 1-3 family houses and individual residential condo units, and conveyances under $500,000, consideration excludes the value of any lien/encumbrance remaining at conveyance.

Additional $1.25 per $500 of consideration applies to conveyances within a city of 1,000,000+ population when residential consideration is $3,000,000 or more (or $2,000,000+ for other property). 'Residential real property' includes a 1-3 family house, an individual condo unit, or a cooperative apartment unit.

Additional ('mansion') tax: 1% of consideration on conveyance of residential real property (1-3 family house, individual condo unit, co-op unit) when consideration for the entire conveyance is $1,000,000 or more. Paid by the grantee; if grantee fails to pay or is exempt, the grantor has the duty to pay and liability is joint and several.

NYS Tax Dept: base transfer tax $2 per $500 of consideration (consideration > $500); additional 'mansion' tax 1% for residences at $1M+. For NYC conveyances from July 1, 2019: extra $1.25 per $500 for residential >= $3M (or other property >= $2M), plus a supplemental tax on residential >= $2M at incremental rates between 0.25% and 2.9% (rates in Form TP-584-NYC-I).
cite: NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' page (reviewed June 1, 2026)

claim: Who pays: base tax and additional base tax are paid by the grantor (seller) (buyer pays if seller doesn't or is exempt); mansion tax and NYC supplemental tax are paid by the buyer (seller pays if buyer fails/is exempt, joint and several).

Except for exemptions in RPL 463, every seller of residential real property under a purchase contract must complete and sign a property condition disclosure statement and deliver it (or a copy) to the buyer or buyer's agent before the buyer signs a binding contract of sale; a copy signed by both parties must be attached to the purchase contract. Parties may still agree to sell 'as is'.

'Residential real property' for the disclosure form means real property improved by a 1-4 family dwelling; it excludes unimproved land, condominium units or cooperative apartments, and HOA property not owned in fee simple by the seller. Form (as of 2025-07-04 revision) includes flood-related questions (FEMA floodplain, flood insurance, elevation certificate, flood claims).

If seller later learns something that makes a previously delivered statement materially inaccurate, seller must deliver a revised statement as soon as practicable, but never required after transfer of title or buyer occupancy, whichever is earlier. Seller is not required to investigate or check public records.

Seller liability: seller who provides (or fails to provide a revised) disclosure statement is liable only for a willful failure to perform the article's requirements, for actual damages plus any other existing equitable or statutory remedy. Article does not limit existing causes of action. The current §465 text (revision 2024-03-29) contains no $500 credit provision.

RPL 463 exempts from the disclosure requirement: court-ordered transfers (incl. probate court transfers, bankruptcy trustee, eminent domain, specific performance), deed in lieu, foreclosure sales and mortgagee resales, transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate/guardianship/conservatorship/trust, transfers between co-owners, to a spouse or lineal relatives, between spouses/former spouses under divorce decree or settlement, to/from government, newly constructed never-inhabited homes, sheriff transfers, and partition actions.

The NY Dept of State's June 2023 PCDS form (dos-1614-f) states that a seller who fails to deliver the statement before the buyer signs a binding contract gives the buyer a $500 credit at title transfer; the 2014 AG opinion also describes the $500 credit (search excerpts only). In residential foreclosure actions involving a home loan where the defendant resides in the property, plaintiff must file proof of service within 20 days of service and the court holds a mandatory settlement conference within 60 days after proof of service is filed with the county clerk (or adjourned date agreed by parties). Purpose includes loan modification, short sale, deed in lieu, other loss mitigation.

Parties must negotiate in good faith. If plaintiff fails, court must at minimum toll interest, costs and fees during undue delay and may impose a civil penalty up to $25,000, compel documents, and award damages/attorney fees. If defendant fails, case is removed from conference calendar. Plaintiff must file notice of discontinuance and vacatur of lis pendens within 90 days after a settlement/modification is fully executed. A defendant who appears at the conference but did not answer is presumed to have a reasonable excuse and may serve an answer within 30 days of initial appearance.

Court sends defendant's info to a DHCR-designated housing counseling agency upon filing of the request for judicial intervention; first conference includes a copy of the Consumer Bill of Rights (RPAPL 1303).

RPAPL 1304: at least 90 days before a lender, assignee or servicer commences legal action (including foreclosure) on a home loan, it must send the borrower a notice in at least 14-point type beginning 'YOU MAY BE AT RISK OF FORECLOSURE', sent by registered or certified mail and first-class mail, in a separate envelope, with a list of at least 5 housing counseling agencies; the notice is a condition precedent to commencing foreclosure. Needed only once per 12 months for same loan/delinquency; the 90-day period does not apply/ceases if borrower files bankruptcy or no longer occupies the home as principal dwelling.

Under RPAPL 1341, in a foreclosure action where part of principal/interest is due and part is not yet due, if defendant pays into court the amount due plus costs and expenses, the court dismisses the complaint if paid before judgment directing sale, or stays proceedings on the judgment if paid after judgment and before sale.
RPAPL 1311: each person whose interest is claimed to be subject and subordinate to the plaintiff's lien shall be made a party defendant in the foreclosure action (list of persons follows in statute).

RPL 226-b governs a residential tenant's right to sublease/assign (sublet consent in 4+ unit dwellings; assignment needs owner's written consent unless lease says otherwise). It does not address sale of a tenant-occupied property; the prompt's cite of 226-b is a sublease statute.

RPL 232-a (NYC): a month-to-month tenant may not be removed for holding over unless landlord served written notice per the 226-c notice period (residential) or at least 30 days before term expiration (non-residential), stating the landlord elects to terminate and will commence summary proceedings.

RPL 232-b (outside NYC): a month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by the tenant (or by landlord only for non-residential tenancy) on at least one month's notice before term expiration; no notice needed to end a definite-term tenancy. Residential landlord notice periods are governed by 226-c.

RPL 226-c: landlord must give written notice of non-renewal or a rent increase of 5% or more: at least 30 days if occupancy/lease term under 1 year; 60 days if 1 to under 2 years; 90 days if more than 2 years / lease term of 2+ years. Untimely notice means tenancy continues on existing terms until the notice period expires. Notice must also state good cause eviction law status (Art. 6-A) per the version effective Aug 18, 2024 to June 15, 2034.

Tenant protections after foreclosure: a successor in interest must give written notice; a tenant of a non-rent-regulated unit may remain for the greater of 90 days from service of notice or the remainder of the lease term (lease term capped at 3 years for tenants not in occupancy at foreclosure commencement; lease must be good faith, rent not substantially below fair market). Successor intending to occupy one unit as primary residence may limit that one unit's tenant to 90 days.

STAR: Basic STAR is for owner-occupied primary residences; income limit $500,000 for the Basic STAR credit ($250,000 for the Basic STAR exemption); based on the first $30,000 of full value. Enhanced STAR is for primary residences of seniors age 65+ with qualifying income of $110,750 or less for the 2026-27 school year and $113,550 or less for 2027-28; based on first $91,700 of full value for 2027-28. STAR applies only to school district taxes (except partly to city taxes in NYC, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers, Syracuse).

STAR registration: register once via the Homeowner Benefit Portal in Individual Online Services; DTF issues the STAR credit payment each year if eligible. New homeowners should register as soon as the home becomes their primary residence. Update registration after ownership change (marriage, divorce, survivorship, trust, etc.); close registration if you sell the property.

Grievance: file Form RP-524 (outside NYC and Nassau) with the assessor or board of assessment review; deadline is Grievance Day, in most communities the fourth Tuesday in May. Exceptions: Suffolk third Tuesday in May; Westchester towns third Tuesday in June; assessing villages typically third Tuesday of February; NYC complaints by March 15 (Class One) / March 1 (others); Nassau March 1. Only the current tentative roll can be grieved; no cost and no lawyer required.

If BAR relief is denied: Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR) for owner-occupied 1-3 family homes (or small vacant land), $30 fee; or tax certiorari in State Supreme Court under Article 7 of the Real Property Tax Law. Both must start within 30 days of filing of the final assessment roll or notice of filing, whichever is later.

RPTL 1110: real property subject to a delinquent tax lien may be redeemed by paying the enforcing officer the lien amount plus lawful charges on or before the end of the redemption period; the redemption period expires two years after lien date, though tax districts may lengthen it for residential/farm property (RPTL 1111) or shorten it to one year for vacant and abandoned residential property (1111-a), and a published notice (1124) may specify a later date.

NYC tax lien sale: City sells unpaid property tax/water-sewer/other charge liens to a single authorized buyer (not the public); it is not a sale of the property but can lead to foreclosure. Lienholder may charge a 5% surcharge plus interest compounded daily at 6% (assessed value <= $250,000), 9% ($250,000-$450,000) or 16% (> $450,000), plus ~$300 admin costs. Foreclosure may begin within one year after the sale if unpaid. Eligibility e.g. 1-family owner-occupied: $5,000 property tax debt (3 years). 2025 sale held June 3, 2025. 5% surcharge waiver for primary-residence owners with combined income no greater than $110,750.
